title: The Blaschka Object Network — Dealer Ecology and Commercial Paperwork Comparator Register
scope: Archival and printed comparators used to distinguish Blaschka-specific distribution practices from broader nineteenth-century natural-history dealership. This register includes the three documented Blaschka dealer routes only when they occur in a shared receiving-side record structure, and also includes non-Blaschka natural-history dealers preserved in the same series or in closely comparable transaction records.
methodological_guard: A comparator is not evidence that a dealer sold Blaschka models. Entries are included because they expose comparable commercial actions such as catalogue circulation, specimen/model selection, approval shipments, invoices, cheques, returns, account reconciliation, insurance, exchange, or museum acquisition paperwork. Blaschka-specific claims remain confined to sources that explicitly identify the models or workshop.

This supports comparative study of dealer correspondence while preserving the distinction between holding-level and item-level evidence.

transaction_process_comparators.collection: John Ruskin letters to Robert Damon

process_evidence.action: customer selects minerals from a dealer shipment, returns the catalogue, and encloses a cheque for retained items
customer requests specimens on approval together with additional goods
customer requests the dealer's catalogue and refers to items kept and returned
customer reconciles the transaction through a list of retained minerals and offers to correct discrepancies

transaction_process_comparators.research_value: This compact sequence exposes Damon's ordinary commercial workflow in the same years as his Blaschka agency: catalogue circulation, approval shipment, selective retention/return, cheque payment, and later reconciliation. It is a control for deciding which features of Blaschka transactions were dealer-standard rather than object-specific.

transaction_process_comparators.research_value: The archival pamphlet advertises Blaschka glass models and identifies Ward as the sole American agent. It is a direct printed witness to how agency status and catalogue access were marketed to customers.
